newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: COLES FALLS AFTER BULLISH FORECASTS DROPPED.
newsitem.headline: COLES FALLS AFTER BULLISH FORECASTS DROPPED.

text.p: Shares in Australia's biggest retailer, Coles Myer Ltd, on Tuesday fell to their lowest ebb in a month after some bullish profit forecasts were apparently scrapped.
Coles shares touched A$6.44 on Tuesday afternoon, their lowest level since July 15, extending a sell-off begun on Monday when they slid 24 cents, or three percent, to close at A$6.59.
A newspaper report on Tuesday said the sell-off followed profit warnings from Coles Myer in private briefings with analysts, prompting some of them to downgrade their forecasts.
Some share analysts had forecast Coles Myer to report a near-record profit of over A$400 million for the year ending July 1998, bringing the average forecast up to A$380 million.
Coles Myer on Tuesday denied giving profit warnings to select analysts. "It's a mystery to me," Coles Myer spokesman Greg Every said of the newspaper report and share price slump.
But analysts said it appeared some of the overly optimistic profit forecasts for Coles Myer, including the top forecast of A$429 million, had been quietly dropped as unrealistic.
"Given the tough conditions and the high (profit) base, A$429 million is off the planet," one analyst told Reuters.
Coles Myer is expected to report net profit before abnormals of between A$360 million and A$370 million for 1997/98, after a 1996/97 profit of around A$330 million, the analysts said.
Coles Myer is due to announce its 1996/97 profit in October.
Prudential-Bache Securities analyst John Burgess said no new information had come to light in recent days to make him revise his forecasts.
"The current economic conditions just don't make that A$429 million attainable," Burgess said.
Australia's retail sector has been in the doldrums over the past year due to persistently high unemployment, low inflation and intense competition for the consumer dollar.
Coles Myer, emerging from a painful profit rut, has begun to lift its bottom line through store revamps, more targetted sales strategies and a move away from discounting wars.
